Pregnancy

Asafoetida in pregnancy: food seasoning and herbal remedies

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Asafoetida, also called hing, is used as a strong-flavoured spice and in herbal remedies for gas or indigestion. Adequate human evidence has not established the safety of medicinal asafoetida products in pregnancy. Avoid self-treating with extracts, capsules or concentrated preparations; a small amount in a meal is a different exposure and is not proof that a miscarriage will occur.

What asafoetida is

Asafoetida is a pungent gum-resin obtained from Ferula plants, including Ferula assa-foetida, in the Apiaceae family, which also includes parsley. The perennial plants have divided leaves and clusters of small flowers. Resin collected from the root or lower stem can harden into pieces or be made into powder; its colour and formulation vary.

A spice blend, pure resin, capsule, extract, oil and tincture are not interchangeable. Check every ingredient: a commercial powder may contain other ingredients, while a concentrated preparation can give a very different exposure. The smell, colour, a natural label or an antioxidant claim cannot establish a safe pregnancy dose.

Traditional uses are not proven pregnancy benefits

Asafoetida has been promoted for gas, indigestion and constipation, and for pain, joint or skin complaints. Other claims include antimicrobial or antifungal effects, immunity, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, kidney stones and jaundice. These claims do not establish effective treatment in a pregnant person, and laboratory antioxidant activity is not a clinical health benefit by itself.

Claims about cancer, asthma or cough, epilepsy, anxiety, depression, sleep, sexual desire, fertility, menstrual pain or bringing on a period also require reliable clinical evidence. Do not replace cancer treatment, antibiotics, inhalers, seizure treatment or mental-health care with asafoetida. Never use it to induce labour, end a pregnancy or manage bleeding at home.

What the digestive trials can and cannot show

Small adult trials published in 2018 and 2025 reported improvements in some digestive symptoms with specific asafoetida formulations. They lasted 30 and 14 days respectively, and excluded pregnant participants. The 2025 trial had manufacturer funding and some authors affiliated with the manufacturer; this matters when assessing the need for independent confirmation.

Short studies in selected adults cannot establish fetal safety, rare harms or a safe pregnancy dose. Results from one formulation cannot be transferred to every spice mixture or supplement. Improvements in symptom scores, sleep or gut bacteria do not prove a treatment for pregnancy-related bloating, depression or other diseases.

Pregnancy uncertainty is different from certain harm

An older experiment found reproductive effects from an extract in pregnant rats. Animal findings and historical use to bring on menstruation raise concern about medicinal use, but cannot quantify the risk from a particular human exposure or prove that every amount in food causes miscarriage or premature labour. Adequate human pregnancy safety data are lacking.

General teratology advice distinguishes moderate use of herbs in cooking from herbal medicines; this is not an asafoetida-specific guarantee. Do not begin concentrated asafoetida remedies during pregnancy or while trying to conceive without specialist advice. There is no established safe medicinal dose here, and increasing the dose to obtain a digestive effect is inappropriate.

If you have already used it

Eating a meal seasoned with asafoetida is not, by itself, evidence that the pregnancy has been harmed. Do not assume that an exposure caused a loss or blame yourself. If you used a remedy, a large or uncertain amount, or an unknown mixture, contact your maternity clinician or pharmacist promptly for an individualized assessment.

Keep the package and record the ingredients, amount, timing, pregnancy stage, symptoms and other medicines. Avoid further doses of an unassessed herbal remedy while seeking advice; do not stop prescribed treatment on your own. If you suspect exposure to a harmful substance or poisoning, seek emergency medical assessment immediately, even without symptoms. If you are unsure whether an exposure is harmful, contact a poison service or urgent medical advice service now. Do not induce vomiting or try a home antidote.

Side effects, interactions and infant safety

The frequency and severity of adverse effects from different asafoetida products are not well defined. Digestive upset, diarrhoea, headache, dizziness or a new rash after a product warrants advice rather than taking more to treat the problem. Pain when urinating, unusual bleeding, marked illness or neurological symptoms need assessment; they should not be dismissed as a harmless herb reaction.

Herbal products can contain variable amounts, contaminants or undeclared ingredients and may affect medicines. Tell the pharmacist about blood thinners, blood-pressure or diabetes medicines, seizure treatment, bleeding disorders and all other supplements; the interaction assessment depends on the actual product and your health. A life-threatening methemoglobinemia case after an asafoetida remedy in an infant supports avoiding such remedies for babies; it does not measure the risk from maternal food seasoning.

Safer ways to discuss gas and constipation

For mild discomfort, try comfortable small meals, drinking water, suitable activity and adequate fibre from a varied diet. Increase fibre gradually if it worsens gas. Constipation is common in pregnancy; if iron seems to contribute, ask about changing the preparation rather than stopping prescribed iron. Do not remove whole food groups or substitute another herb without advice.

Persistent bloating, indigestion or constipation deserves a discussion with your maternity clinician or pharmacist about the cause and pregnancy-appropriate options. Reflux, constipation and other problems need different care, and a medicine being suitable in pregnancy does not guarantee relief. Do not assume every abdominal pain is trapped wind, and keep routine antenatal appointments.

When symptoms need urgent help

Contact maternity care immediately for abdominal pain with spotting or bleeding, regular cramps or tightenings, unusual discharge or leaking fluid, lower back pain, or urinary symptoms. Persistent pain, fever, or severe headache or visual changes with upper abdominal pain also needs urgent assessment. Possible pregnancy with new one-sided lower abdominal pain needs urgent advice even without a positive test.

Severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding, needs emergency care now. Breathing difficulty or lip, tongue or throat swelling after a product, a seizure, blue or grey lips, or inability to wake also needs immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself and do not delay assessment to try a digestive remedy. Pelvic pain that hurts when you move or touch the area, or pelvic pain with sudden confusion, also needs immediate emergency care; do not wait for other signs.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

MotherToBaby and NIH ODS distinguish evidence limitations and product variability from assurances based on natural origin. Moderate food use is a different exposure from medicinal preparations; there is no established asafoetida pregnancy dose.

The 2004 rat experiment raises a reproductive-safety concern without measuring human culinary risk. The 2018 and 2025 adult digestive trials excluded pregnancy; short-term tolerability is not fetal-safety evidence. The infant toxicity report is a case report, not an estimate of risk from maternal food.

NHS advice supports checking remedies and medicines, practical constipation care, and prompt assessment of concerning pregnancy pain, poisoning or allergy symptoms. Herbal products must not replace antenatal or condition-specific treatment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record products, symptoms and questions for a maternity appointment. It cannot establish that a herbal product is safe, predict an individual pregnancy outcome or diagnose the cause of pain. The closed spice jar illustrates a question about ingredients, without showing consumption or a recommended dose.

When to seek help

Avoid self-treatment with concentrated asafoetida products and do not use herbs to induce labour or end a pregnancy. Do not stop prescribed medicines or give asafoetida remedies to babies. If you suspect exposure to a harmful substance or poisoning, seek emergency medical assessment immediately, even without symptoms. If you are unsure whether an exposure is harmful, contact a poison service or urgent medical advice service now. Do not induce vomiting or try a home antidote. Severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy vaginal bleeding, needs immediate emergency help. Breathing or throat-swelling reactions, seizure, blue or grey lips or inability to wake also needs emergency help; do not drive yourself. Pelvic pain that hurts when you move or touch the area, or pelvic pain with sudden confusion, also needs immediate emergency care; do not wait for other signs.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Food seasoning and concentrated asafoetida remedies are different exposures; neither a natural label nor an animal study defines a safe medicinal pregnancy dose.
  • Small digestive trials in nonpregnant adults do not establish fetal safety or justify self-treatment in pregnancy.
  • One meal containing asafoetida is not proof of harm; seek individualized advice for a remedy, uncertain amount, symptoms or possible poisoning.
  • Discuss side effects, medicines and product ingredients with a clinician or pharmacist, and do not give asafoetida remedies to infants.
  • Use practical pregnancy-appropriate care for mild digestive symptoms and seek urgent help for pain, bleeding or emergency warning signs.

Frequently asked questions

What is asafoetida, or hing?

It is a strongly scented gum-resin from Ferula plants, used as a spice and in herbal products. Pure resin, mixed culinary powders, capsules and extracts can have different ingredients and concentrations; they are not interchangeable.

Are its advertised medicinal properties proven?

Traditional uses and laboratory antioxidant or antimicrobial findings do not prove clinical benefit. Some small adult digestive trials are available, but they do not establish effective pregnancy treatment or justify using it for cancer, epilepsy, asthma, diabetes, mood problems or fertility.

Is asafoetida safe in pregnancy?

Adequate human evidence has not established the safety of medicinal use or a safe dose. Avoid self-treatment with concentrated products. Moderate culinary use is a different exposure, but general advice about herbs in food is not a specific guarantee for every asafoetida product.

Does it have a proven benefit for pregnancy bloating?

No reliable pregnancy-specific benefit has been established. The small digestive trials excluded pregnant participants. Discuss persistent symptoms and pregnancy-appropriate options rather than taking a trial dose or replacing the herb with another unassessed remedy.

Will one seasoned meal cause a miscarriage?

It is not evidence that a miscarriage will occur. Rat extract experiments cannot predict the outcome of one human meal. If the amount or mixture was unusual or uncertain, or symptoms occur, seek individualized advice; do not blame yourself or induce vomiting.

What side effects or interactions should I watch for?

The risks vary with the product and are incompletely characterized. New rash, troublesome digestive symptoms, dizziness or unusual bleeding needs advice before further use. Tell a pharmacist about all medicines and bleeding or seizure disorders. Breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, fainting or loss of consciousness, seizure or blue lips needs emergency care.

Can I give it to a baby for colic?

Do not give asafoetida herbal remedies to infants. A published case describes life-threatening methemoglobinemia after ingestion, affecting the blood’s oxygen-carrying function. A baby with blue or grey lips, breathing difficulty or difficulty waking needs emergency help now.

When should I seek care instead of treating gas?

Contact maternity care immediately for abdominal pain with bleeding, regular tightenings, leaking fluid or urinary symptoms. Severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding, needs immediate emergency care. A possible pregnancy with new one-sided pain needs urgent advice even without a positive test. Pelvic pain that hurts when you move or touch the area, or pelvic pain with sudden confusion, also needs immediate emergency care; do not wait for other signs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
